units.t: Rocks, the rock cycle and soil

unit.title: Rocks, the rock cycle and soil
unit.blurb: How igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form, how rocks keep changing, and what soil is made of.

O1.t: Describe how igneous rocks form from magma and lava, and link crystal size to how fast the rock cooled.

O2.t: Use a simple key and observations to identify rocks.

O3.t: Describe weathering, erosion and sedimentation, and how sedimentary rocks and fossils form.

O4.t: Describe how heat and pressure form metamorphic rocks, and describe the rock cycle.

O5.t: Link the uses of rocks to their properties.

O6.t: Describe what soil is made of and compare sandy soil, clay soil and loam.

O7.t: Carry out a fair test of how well soils drain, and describe how people can improve or harm soil.

captions: Hello, rock scientists!
This is lesson 3.1: igneous rocks.
Let's look inside the Earth.
On the outside is the crust, where we live.
Under the crust is the mantle. Parts of it are so hot that rock melts.
Melted rock under the ground is called magma.
Sometimes magma pushes up through the crust and comes out of a volcano.
When magma reaches the surface, we call it lava.
The lava cools down and becomes solid rock. This is called solidification.
Rock that forms when magma or lava cools and becomes solid is called igneous rock.
Igneous means made from fire!
Igneous rocks are made of crystals that fit tightly together. They are hard and do not let water through.
Pause and think. What is lava?
Lava cools quickly on the Earth's surface. The crystals have no time to grow, so they are tiny. These are extrusive igneous rocks, like basalt.
Magma that cools slowly deep underground grows big crystals that you can see with the naked eye. These are intrusive igneous rocks, like granite.
Your turn. Why does granite have big crystals?
Geologists use keys to identify rocks.
Look closely: can you see the crystals with your naked eye?
If yes, it is an intrusive igneous rock, like granite.
If no, it is an extrusive igneous rock, like basalt.
Igneous rocks are strong and hard-wearing.
Granite is used for buildings and kitchen tops.
Crushed basalt is used to make roads.
And pumice, a rock full of gas holes, is so light it can float!
Let's remember.
Magma is melted rock underground. Lava is magma on the surface.
Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools and becomes solid.
Quick cooling makes small crystals. Slow cooling makes big crystals.
Granite and basalt are igneous rocks.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, rock scientists!
This is lesson 3.2: sedimentary rocks and fossils.
Rocks on the surface slowly break into smaller pieces.
Rain, ice, wind, changes in temperature and plant roots all crack rocks.
This breaking down is called weathering.
Rivers, wind and ice carry the broken pieces away.
This is called erosion, and the moving is called transport.
As they tumble along, the pieces become smaller and rounder.
These bits of rock, sand and mud are called sediment.
When the river slows down, for example in a lake or the sea, the sediment sinks to the bottom.
This is called sedimentation, or deposition.
Layer after layer builds up over millions of years.
The heavy top layers squash the bottom layers, and they stick together to form sedimentary rock.
Pause and think. Can you put these in order: sedimentation, weathering, erosion?
Sandstone is made of sand grains stuck together.
Shale is made of mud, and splits into thin layers.
Limestone is often made from tiny shells.
Sedimentary rocks have layers and grains, and many let water soak in.
Sometimes a plant or animal dies and is quickly covered by sediment.
The soft parts rot away, but hard parts like bones and shells are buried.
Over a very long time, minerals replace them and they turn to stone.
These are fossils. They are found in sedimentary rocks.
Your turn. In which type of rock do we find fossils?
You can model sedimentation in a jar.
Put gravel, sand and soil in a jar of water, and shake it.
Leave it to settle for a day.
The heaviest pieces sink first, so you will see layers, just like in sedimentary rock.
Let's remember.
Weathering breaks rocks into small pieces.
Erosion carries the pieces away as sediment.
Layers of sediment are squashed together to form sedimentary rock.
And fossils are found in sedimentary rocks.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello again, rock scientists!
This is lesson 3.3: metamorphic rocks and the rock cycle.
Deep underground, rocks can be buried under other rocks.
There they are heated and squeezed by huge pressure.
They do not melt, but their crystals change and line up.
The rock becomes a new kind of rock, called metamorphic rock. Metamorphic means changed in shape.
Limestone changes into marble, a beautiful rock used for statues.
Shale changes into slate, which splits into flat sheets for roofs.
And granite can change into gneiss, which has stripes of crystals.
Pause and think. What two things change rocks into metamorphic rocks?
Rocks are always slowly changing from one type to another. This is called the rock cycle.
Igneous rock is weathered and eroded into sediment, which becomes sedimentary rock.
Buried rock is heated and squeezed into metamorphic rock.
If rock melts, it becomes magma, which cools to make new igneous rock. And the cycle goes on and on.
Your turn. What happens when a metamorphic rock melts?
We can model the rock cycle with old wax crayons.
Grate the crayons into shavings, like weathering. Press them together, like sedimentary rock.
Warm them a little in your hands and press hard, like metamorphic rock.
With an adult, melt them and let them cool, like igneous rock.
Look around your town.
You may find marble floors, slate roofs, limestone walls and granite steps.
Each rock is chosen because of its properties.
Let's remember.
Heat and pressure change rocks into metamorphic rocks.
Limestone becomes marble, and shale becomes slate.
The rock cycle changes rocks from one type to another.
And it takes millions of years.
Great job! See you in the practice room.

captions: Hello, scientists!
This is lesson 3.4: soil.
Soil is the top layer of the ground, where plants grow.
It is made of tiny pieces of weathered rock, mixed with air, water and organic matter.
Organic matter, also called humus, comes from dead and rotting plants and animals.
Sandy soil has big grains. Water drains through it quickly, so it dries out.
Clay soil has tiny grains and feels sticky. It holds lots of water and can become waterlogged.
Loam is a mixture of sand, clay and humus. It is the best soil for most plants.
Pause and think. Which type of soil is best for most plants?
Let's test how quickly water drains through different soils.
Use the same amount of each soil, and pour in the same amount of water.
Measure how much water drips through in five minutes.
Sandy soil lets the most water through. Clay soil lets the least through.
Here are our results.
Eighty millilitres drained through the sandy soil, but only fifteen through the clay.
So sandy soil drains fastest.
Farmers and gardeners can improve soil.
Adding compost adds humus and nutrients that help plants grow.
But too much artificial fertiliser and pesticide can harm living things in the soil and in rivers.
Your turn. What does compost add to the soil?
Let's remember.
Soil is weathered rock mixed with humus, air and water.
Sandy soil drains fast, and clay soil holds water.
Loam is best for most plants.
And compost makes soil better.
Well done! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
